title: Kochi to Set Up Seven Air Quality Monitors as Pollution Concern Mounts
excerpt: Kochi Corporation plans seven new monitoring stations for Rs 10 lakh as two of the pollution board's three continuous stations have been down for over six months, leaving only Eloor operational.
body:
• Kochi Corporation plans seven new air quality monitoring stations, budgeted at ₹10 lakh, with technical support from SCMS School of Engineering and Technology, Mirror Now reported.
  • Two of the Kerala pollution board's three continuous monitoring stations in the city — at Vyttila and Kaloor — have been out of service for more than six months; only the Eloor station remains fully operational.
  • Tentative sites include the Corporation office, Edappally, Vyttila, Thoppumpady and Fort Kochi, subject to council approval, with a public dashboard expected within the next two months.
  • Kerala's Chief Minister said the state's AQI concern extends to Kochi, where AQI has crossed 188, and an expert committee will be formed this month to recommend urgent measures.

Concern is mounting over poor air quality in Kochi, and the Kochi Corporation is moving to set up seven new air quality monitoring stations across the city to provide residents with real-time data on local pollution levels, Mirror Now reported, in coverage of the plan first reported by The Hindu.

The push comes as the city grapples with a noticeable decline in its Air Quality Index, a trend that has sparked public debate and anxiety, Mirror Now said. Experts cited in that report suggested the transition from monsoon to winter — shifting wind patterns and lower temperatures trapping pollutants at surface level — alongside human factors such as heavy vehicular emissions, unmanaged construction sites and improper waste disposal.

A monitoring gap at the centre of the story

The immediate problem is not only pollution, but measurement. Two of Kochi's three Continuous Ambient Air Quality Monitoring Stations run by the Kerala State Pollution Control Board, at Vyttila and Kaloor, have been out of service for more than six months, Mirror Now reported. The board is awaiting state government approval to proceed with repairs, after the previous maintenance agency ceased operations and a new tender drew only a single bidder.

A senior board official noted that the board continues manual air quality monitoring at five locations to report to the Central Pollution Control Board, but the lack of real-time data from Vyttila and Kaloor remains a challenge. Only the station at Eloor remains fully operational.

What the Corporation plans

The Corporation's project is budgeted at ₹10 lakh and will be executed with technical support from the SCMS School of Engineering and Technology, according to Mirror Now. Mayor V.K. Minimol said the initiative was included in the municipal budget to address public unease. Tentative sites include the Corporation office, Edappally, Vyttila, Thoppumpady and Fort Kochi, with final locations subject to council approval. A public-facing dashboard is expected within the next two months.

S. Abhilash, director of the Cusat Radar Centre, emphasised in the same report that pollution levels are highly localised, and that the chemical particulate matter in industrial areas such as Eloor differs from pollutants in traffic-heavy hubs such as Vyttila. Experts agreed scientific source-apportionment studies are needed to pinpoint exact causes.

The wider state response

At the concluding day of the two-day Future Kochi Conclave, jointly organised by the Kochi Municipal Corporation, Jain University and Cardiff University, Chief Minister V.D. Satheesan said the government viewed Kochi's AQI, which has crossed 188, with utmost seriousness, and that an expert committee will be constituted this month to study urban air pollution and recommend urgent remedial measures, the Press Network of India reported. He said the city must not be allowed to reach a situation similar to Delhi's, and pointed to reducing private vehicles entering the city and building an integrated public transport network connecting bus, metro and water transport.

Why residents should care about the readings

Air pollution's health effects are the reason local, reliable readings matter. The World Health Organization's guidance on air pollution and health says pollutants with the strongest evidence for adverse outcomes include particulate matter PM2.5 and PM10, ozone, nitrogen dioxide, sulphur dioxide and carbon monoxide, and that air pollution has an especially devastating impact on children's health. Until Kochi's continuous stations are repaired and the new stations are live, residents in neighbourhoods far from Eloor have no real-time official reading for their own area — which is the gap the Corporation says its seven stations are meant to close.
